hints.hint: Turn every condition, including a remark about what someone knows, into an explicit constraint: an equation, a divisibility, an inequality, a bound. Impose them in order, and on BOTH members of any pair -- mutual requirements are severe and often force the symmetric case where two unknowns coincide, so test that case, not only lopsided ones. Prefer structure (factorizations, bounds, parity, symmetry) over long case lists; keep exact integers. Before discarding a candidate that met every stated condition, audit the discard: you probably added a fact the text never gave, or settled a choice the wording leaves open. Never report a value your own work refuted, and never call the problem broken. Verify by recomputing the requested quantity a second, independent way; when the two routes agree, state that result and stop.
hints.mutation: replace the abstract intersect-across-readings clause with an audit-before-discarding rule plus a both-members/symmetric-case test and a second-independent-route verification
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent scored 0/8; two rollouts hit the 16384 cap and all eight burned 13.4k-16.4k tokens, one repeating 'impossible' 130 times. The decisive evidence: six rollouts explicitly constructed the balanced pair where the two picks coincide, verified it against the stated conditions, then talked themselves out of it on a self-invented knowledge claim and reported a factor of the shown number instead. So the binding failure is no longer a missing concept or bad ordering but discarding a candidate that already passed. The incumbent's intersect-across-live-readings clause is too abstract to fire before the budget is gone, so I replaced it with an audit-the-discard rule, an explicit demand to impose each constraint on both members of the pair (which surfaces the symmetric case), and a concrete second-route verification as the stopping condition.

hints.hint:
Divide by the appropriate power of the variable to introduce the ratio w=(z-1)/z; the equation then pins w to a finite set on a circle. Solve for z in terms of w and turn the locus into an equation in x and y, completing the square to read off center and radius. Generally: substitute so the relation depends on one quantity, and keep every value exact.

Guard the steps that are not reversible. Note where a divisor vanishes before dividing; after squaring or clearing denominators, test candidates in the original relation and drop the ones it fails. If a quantity you assumed constant comes out varying, your assumed form was too narrow, not the problem broken: widen it and fit the general shape rather than re-auditing sound algebra. Record your simplified result as soon as you have one; never restart.
hints.mutation: replace the generic clashing-check clause with (a) an irreversible-step guard (divisor zeros, extraneous roots after squaring/clearing) and (b) a widen-the-assumed-form rule for when a supposedly constant quantity comes out varying
hints.subagent_summary: Only 6 of 8 fresh rollouts scored; both failures hit the 16384-token cap with no stated value. Both derived the correct reduction and then computed the modulus of each root, found it varying, and concluded the setup or the problem must be broken - they spent thousands of tokens relitigating sound algebra. One eventually recovered the general conic form and verified it, but too late to report. The real defect is a too-narrow assumption (an origin-centered locus, i.e. constant modulus) being read as a contradiction. So I replaced the incumbent's vague recheck-that-line advice with a concrete widen-the-assumed-form rule, plus a transferable guard on the irreversible steps (vanishing divisors, extraneous roots from squaring or clearing denominators) that generate such conflicts elsewhere.

hints.hint: Fix one setup and never rebuild it. Overlapping or double-counted pieces obey total = sum minus overlap, so maximize coverage by minimizing overlap; the same bookkeeping serves counting. A vertex reaches only the directions inside its own angle, so being larger never proves one object swallows another; the shared part stays strictly between nothing and everything. Never let a size comparison or a plausible round fraction replace a quantity you have not computed. Compute the simplest configuration exactly, where boundaries meet at points you read off in one step, and keep that number. Then close with a bound, not a search: sampled values never exclude the ones you skipped, so give one inequality valid in every configuration that your number attains. Bound plus witness is a proof; remaining cases teach nothing. Do the sum-minus-overlap arithmetic in your first visible line and state the result next. Never append a section asking whether another configuration wins.
hints.mutation: generalize the containment trap to a bigger-never-swallows rule with a no-uncomputed-ratios ban, and swap the qualitative trade test for exact simplest-case computation plus a bound-and-witness stop licence
hints.subagent_summary: Six of eight scored, so the sum-minus-overlap frame is kept. Both failures were geometric, not budget: one concluded that because every side of the large piece sits distance 1 from its center while the small piece reaches only 0.5, the small piece is swallowed at every angle, so it reported the plain larger area and stopped early with tokens to spare; the other never closed reasoning, oscillating between whole-piece and partial overlap while re-testing tilts. The incumbent's wedge sentence and its qualitative enters-vs-leaves trade test did not block either. This revision states the containment trap as a general rule (bigger never implies swallowing, and a ratio or a round-looking fraction is not a computed quantity), replaces the trade test with compute-the-simplest-configuration-exactly, and supplies a bound-plus-witness reason that licenses halting.

hints.hint:
For "at most how many" questions give both halves: an upper bound and an example reaching it. Name a count early, before you run long.

Bound recipe worth reusing: name the scarce resource, cap what ONE unit of it can cover, then multiply by the number of units. Neither the per-unit cap nor the unit count is the total by itself.

For function pieces: posit ONE unknown affine target for the whole pattern (an arithmetic progression is A+B*n), shared by every piece; index n suits piece f exactly when the residual f(x)-(A+Bx) vanishes at n. Never demand one piece alone give consecutive terms - neighbours may come from different pieces, and reuse is allowed unless forbidden. Subtracting a line leaves the leading term, so the residual keeps the full stated degree d: d roots per piece, never d-1.

Attain it with consecutive blocks, one piece each.
hints.mutation: generalize the cap into a reusable scarce-resource recipe (cap one unit, multiply by unit count) and add a degree audit pinning the per-piece cap at d rather than d-1
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh rollouts: 3/8 correct. Two failures capped each piece at d-1 roots instead of the stated degree d - an off-by-one in the residual step. Two more abandoned reuse entirely and reported the bare piece count, one after first declaring the count unbounded. One burned all tokens chasing consecutive-difference relations between neighbouring pieces. The three winners all ran the same route: shared affine target, residual roots per piece, multiply by the piece count. So the incumbent's structure is right but two numeric slips survive it. This revision lifts the bound step into a reusable recipe (name the scarce resource, cap one unit, multiply by the unit count) so it transfers past polynomials, adds an explicit degree audit pinning the per-piece cap at d rather than d-1, and states that reuse is permitted unless forbidden to block the retreat to the bare piece count.

hints.hint: Name your unknowns and turn each given condition into one exact equation; solve for any constants first. Reduce to a single variable, keep exact fractions, and discard roots that are degenerate or outside the domain. Read every logarithm, exponent, or root off its definition -- which power of the base gives this value -- and remember a base below one flips the sign; one such slip masquerades as an inconsistent problem, so recheck it instead of looping. Verify a candidate by substituting it back into the original conditions, not by re-deriving; once it passes, stop revisiting it. Re-read the question and report the exact quantity it asks for, simplified. State your result early, then stop.
hints.mutation: add evaluate-from-the-definition rule for logs/exponents (base below one flips the sign) and reframe an apparent inconsistency as that slip rather than a reason to loop
hints.subagent_summary: Six of eight fresh rollouts were correct; both failures ran to the token cap on the same mechanical error, not on strategy. Each set up the conditions correctly, solved the reduced quadratic correctly, kept the right root, then evaluated a logarithm with base below one with the wrong sign. The bad value made the recovered vertex fail the substitution check, so the rollout concluded the problem itself was inconsistent and spent thousands of tokens re-expanding the identical algebra, which can never surface an evaluation slip. The incumbent already mandates substitute-back verification but says nothing about what to do when it fails, so I added a transferable rule: evaluate logs/exponents/roots from the definition rather than by pattern-copying, note that a base under one reverses the sign, and treat an apparent contradiction as that slip.

hints.hint:
Trap: a process random over MOVES is rarely uniform over OUTCOMES. "Each item equally likely in each position", "equally likely to go last", "n! orderings so 1/n!" are guesses, not derivations.

Build ONE sample space and reuse it for EVERY part: the genuinely FREE 50/50 steps. A step is 1/2 only when both options are legal, forced steps count 1. Get that count by walking legality, not by counting items.

WHICH item a step carries is fixed by the earlier steps, never an independent draw. A pile grows upward, so depth k is an EARLY arrival: "named item at depth k" pins a short OPENING block of steps. Multiply 1/2 over the free steps in that block instead of enumerating runs.

A surprisingly small value is no evidence against itself; two parts may share one value.
hints.mutation: state that which item a step carries is determined by earlier steps (never an independent draw), and route a named-item-at-depth-k event through a short opening block of steps rather than the choose-between-two-readings trace
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent gave 0/8; seven rollouts stopped normally at 7k-15k tokens, so length is not the block. Five of eight reached the free-step count on part one, then every rollout priced the slot part by asserted symmetry, reading off 1/n (or 1/2, or 3!/6 of 4!), and each had first equated the deepest slot with whatever moved last. One collapsed the whole process to certainty and then impossibility. The incumbent asks the student to write both readings of the slot and kill one by tracing a run; it picks a reading and never traces. This revision drops that step and instead states the causal fact the failures violate -- which item a step carries is fixed by the earlier steps, never an independent uniform draw -- gives the upward-growth orientation declaratively, and turns the slot event into a short opening block of steps to price, so the same denominator serves both parts.

hints.hint: An unlanded derivation scores nothing: get a result written down early, then spend what is left testing it against the conditions exactly as given. Fix notation once and keep the symbol you sum over strictly apart from the index that changes from one condition to the next; collapsing those two turns a sound problem into an apparent contradiction. Hand-solve the smallest honest instance by plain elimination and treat those numbers as ground truth: when a general form clashes with them, your translation slipped, so recheck which symbol plays which role instead of re-deriving the instance or doubting the statement. To pull out one wanted coefficient, evaluate or substitute at a convenient point -- never expand a long product or chase sums over all subsets of roots, which cannot close in your budget. Read a short confirmed list by ratio as well as difference so factorial growth shows, watching sign and any off-by-one shift.
hints.mutation: add a notation-separation rule (summation label vs condition index) plus a ban on long-product / subset-sum coefficient extraction in favor of evaluating at a convenient point, keeping hand-solved instances as the arbiter over any general form
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling scored 1 of 8; 5 of 8 hit the token cap and the 3 that landed were wrong. The dominant wreck is a notation collapse: rollouts conflated the label being summed over with the index that varies across conditions, so their small hand-solved instance clashed with their own general form. They then either re-derived the same tiny case for thousands of tokens or declared the stated system inconsistent. A second sink is coefficient extraction by brute force: several tried to expand a 2000-plus-factor product or sum products of roots taken all-but-one at a time and never closed. The single success stayed on verified numbers and read the growth rate off them. The incumbent already demands early commitment and small cases but never says how to keep the translation straight or how to lift out one coefficient cheaply, so this revision supplies both.

hints.hint: Let H be the total number of houses. The equal-street layout constrains H arithmetically, and integer stage costs per house mean H must divide every listed stage total. Determine the admissible common divisors using the intended maximum-feasible-count interpretation. Add all construction costs before dividing by H, and apply the stated markup multiplicatively. In general, before improvising algebra, classify the problem and reach for the standard tool that class calls for: Vieta or factoring for polynomial roots, similar triangles and the Pythagorean relation for geometry, residues and divisibility for whole-number conditions, complementary counting for enumeration, telescoping for sums. When a direct attack stalls, work the smallest cases by hand and read off the pattern or invariant rather than pushing a long computation. State your result plainly as soon as you have it, then check it once.
hints.mutation: replace the never-exercised exact-fractions clause with an untried problem-type classification plus canonical-tool recall rule
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 fresh rollouts scored reward 1 with clean stops, so train is saturated at 1.0 for the 13th round running and there is no train signal left; every gain must come from transfer, where the incumbent sits at 0.2. The rollouts show the student never exercises the exact-fractions clause (all stage costs are integers and no fraction survives), so that sentence is dead weight and safe to swap. Nineteen rounds of scope-labeling, anti-rumination, output-form, arithmetic-reliability, backward-reasoning and concretization variants all failed to beat it, so I tried the one broadly-applicable move not yet attempted: name the problem class first and recall the canonical tool for that class, since a 1.7B student mostly loses by improvising ad-hoc algebra where a standard technique applies.

hints.hint: Never name unknown coefficients and never expand a composed or high-degree identity; that exhausts your budget. Find structure first. For same-degree maps agreeing for all x, recenter about one shared unknown center c: f=c+a(x-c)^k, g=c-a(x-c)^k, odd k, opposite signs, no offset, so the identity collapses by symmetry. Data symmetric about a center is your lever: adding the two supplied values cancels the a-term and pins c; subtracting isolates a. A degenerate center is one slipped sign, not refutation: fix that line, never by expanding. An input equal to c or a fixed point is immediate. Lacking symmetry, compute the smallest cases by hand and read the invariant off them instead of general algebra. Ugly numbers mean a dropped condition; reread the statement. Verify structurally, commit early.
hints.mutation: compress redundant branch/offset/irrational-center warnings and reinvest in two general guards: a no-symmetry fallback (small concrete cases, extract the invariant) and an ugly-numbers-means-dropped-condition reread rule
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 fresh rollouts were correct, each terminating cleanly at 4.1k-8.2k tokens by committing to the shared-center antisymmetric pair, pinning the center by summing the two supplied values, then evaluating inside the centered form. Train is saturated and no failure mode remains to target, so with transfer weighted double the only lever is generality. The revision compresses the redundant branch/offset and irrational-center warnings (the same slip is already covered by the degenerate-center clause) and spends the freed tokens on two guards that fire on problems with no commuting-map structure: when no symmetry exists, work the smallest concrete cases and extract the invariant instead of grinding general algebra; and treat ugly numbers as a signal that a stated condition was dropped, prompting a reread rather than more computation.

hints.hint: Prefer literal computation to compact notation. Run the stated procedure on the smallest instance step by step, each step acting on the state the previous step produced, never on the original data, and write the whole state after each step. That worked run outranks any formula, notation, or claim about structure; on conflict drop that language rather than repairing it, and never suspect the run. Never accept a count you did not carry out. When asked for the smallest amount achieving something, test your candidate directly: check that it works and that one less fails. Cheap guesses like "two passes undo it" die under that test. Do this at two sizes, then require one expression in the parameter to move with that parameter and reproduce both; if it misses one, shift the exponent, not the instances. Repeating a line, or calling the setup confusing, means stop and state what your instances support.
hints.mutation: add a direct minimality test (confirm the candidate works and that one less fails) so untraced small-period claims are refuted instead of re-audited
hints.subagent_summary: Only 3 of 8 rollouts were right. Every failure asserted a repetition count it never ran: three read a count off untraced cycle-type talk (period equals the step count, or one less than the parameter), one guessed a wildly larger power, and two burned the whole budget looping after a bogus 'two passes suffice' claim they kept re-auditing instead of killing. The incumbent already demands a literal run, but says nothing about testing minimality, so the students accepted the first plausible-looking count. The revision keeps the run-outranks-notation core and adds a concrete minimality test: verify the candidate works and that one less does not, which cheaply refutes the small-period guesses that dominate these failures.
